title: Containers and the Reproducible Deployment

sections.title: Finding Containers That Hit Their Limits

html:
“It works on my machine.” Almost every engineer has said it or heard it, usually just after a deployment failed somewhere else. The sentence is often true. Both machines may run the same Git commit, but they can still differ in library versions, language runtime, configuration values, or credentials, and any one of those differences can stop the application from starting.

Baodium met this problem during a Catalog Service deployment. The release record named one Git commit for the whole fleet, yet some instances started normally and others crashed during startup. Comparing a healthy host with a failing one revealed an older system library, an older Python runtime, and a missing environment variable. The team could repair each host by hand, but the next release would find the next difference.

The lasting fix was to build one versioned container image and promote that same artifact from testing to production. The image would carry the application and its runtime dependencies. Configuration, secrets, resource limits, and Kubernetes lifecycle settings would still come from outside the image, and the rest of this chapter is about making those parts just as dependable.

Source Revision and Runtime Dependencies

A Git revision identifies a source tree. It does not identify the Python interpreter installed on a host, the native library loaded by a package, or the configuration injected when the process starts.

For example, a Python dependency may call a compiled library. The application can import successfully on one host and fail on another because the required version of that library is missing, and a successful start on the first host tells you nothing about the second. These differences between hosts are often called environment drift. The failure may be completely repeatable on each affected host, even though it seems random when engineers compare only application revisions.

Baodium divided the runtime inputs into those that should travel with the application and those the deployment supplies (Table Table).

The image packages one portion of the runtime contract.
Packaged with the application Supplied at deployment or runtime
Application files and dependencies Configuration and secret references
Language runtime and user-space libraries Host kernel and CPU architecture
Default filesystem layout and permissions Mounted files and writable storage
Default process identity and startup command Resource limits, networking, and platform policy

A container image contains the packaged files and default execution settings.1 A running container is a process, or a group of processes, started from that image with additional runtime configuration. On Linux, those processes run directly on the host’s kernel, so the image supplies the user-space environment, such as libraries and utilities, but not a kernel of its own. This is the key difference from a virtual machine. Nothing is emulated, so starting a container is closer to starting a process than to booting a machine, and a kernel-level difference between hosts still reaches inside the container.

This division makes investigations much more precise. If two instances run the same platform-specific image, you can compare their configuration, mounts, limits, and host conditions without first reconstructing every application dependency.

Container Image Builds

The Catalog team changed its release process so that continuous integration (CI) built the application and its user-space dependencies into an image. Hosts no longer installed those dependencies themselves during deployment. Listing Listing shows a simplified Dockerfile.

The base image supplies the Python runtime and its user-space dependencies, and pinning it by digest fixes the base content the build uses. The lock file fixes every application dependency version, including transitive ones, and lists hashes for the permitted package files, so the build fails if a package changes unexpectedly.

The service files are copied by name instead of copying everything in the working directory. That reduces the chance of including local credentials, test output, or unrelated files, and the build context’s ignore file excludes them as well. The numeric user runs the service without root privileges, so the files needed at runtime must be readable by that user and any directories it writes to must have suitable ownership.

The final command uses the exec form, so the container starts Python directly rather than through a shell. This matters for shutdown, because a shell wrapper can stop termination signals from reaching the application unless it replaces itself with the application process. A second trap is less obvious. Inside a container, the first process runs with process ID (PID) 1, and Linux ignores termination signals sent to PID 1 unless that process has installed a handler for them. Python does not install a handler for SIGTERM by default, so a service like this one must either handle the signal itself or run under a small init process such as tini. Otherwise, the signal is ignored and the platform eventually kills the process without any chance to finish its requests.

Test the built image itself, including its permissions, startup command, native libraries, packaged files, and signal handling. Unit tests that run directly on the CI host never touch them.

Reproducible Container Build Inputs

Pinning makes a build predictable, but it also means that nothing changes until someone rebuilds the image. A security patch published today reaches production only after a rebuild. Fixing dependency versions makes builds repeatable. A regular rebuild and review process is still necessary to incorporate subsequent security updates. Most teams solve this with a recurring job, or a tool such as Dependabot or Renovate, that updates the fixed version references, runs the tests, and opens a change for review. Dependency updates then arrive regularly as ordinary reviewed changes instead of relying on someone’s memory.

A patched base image leaves existing images untouched. Only a rebuild picks up the fix. The team updates the approved base reference, rebuilds, tests, and publishes a new artifact, and the same applies to fixes in application dependencies.

Build tools can introduce further inputs. If installing a package compiles native code, the compiler version and build dependencies matter too. A multi-stage build handles this well. One stage contains the compilers and build tools, and the final image receives only the runtime files copied from it, which also makes the final image smaller and gives an attacker fewer tools to work with.

The release record includes the source revision, the base-image reference, a dependency inventory, and build provenance. An image digest identifies content, but it does not tell you who built the image or whether it passed the required checks. Signing images and recording their provenance, for example with Sigstore’s cosign, lets the deployment platform verify those facts before it runs an image.

Image Promotion by Digest

Once CI has built and tested an image, the release pipeline needs to identify that exact artifact. Figure Figure contrasts building a separate image for each environment with building once and promoting that one image.

A tag such as catalog-service:release-42 is like a nickname. It is convenient, but depending on registry policy, someone can give the same nickname to a different image. A digest is more like a fingerprint, calculated from the image content, so it always refers to the same content. That gives you a simple rule. Deploy by digest, for example catalog-service@sha256:…, and use tags only as labels for people.

Baodium recorded the published digest in the release manifest and promoted that reference through test, staging, and production. Production never rebuilt the image from the source revision.

Why insist on promoting one image if the source has not changed? A second build can pick up a changed base image, resolve a different package version, use another compiler, or include different generated metadata. Testing one build tells you nothing certain about a later build from the same source, any more than tasting one cake tells you about the next. Promoting the recorded artifact removes that uncertainty from the release path. Getting identical output from a repeated build is a separate goal, known as a reproducible build, and it requires control over every relevant build input.

Multi-platform images add one more detail. A single image index can refer to separate images for different CPU architectures, so a fleet that runs on both x86 and ARM hosts needs to test each platform-specific image and record which one each instance runs. The release pipeline also checks the deployed digest to confirm which image a requested tag resolved to, and the registry’s retention policy retains previously approved artifacts for rollback.

Configuration Outside the Image

Database endpoints, feature settings, credentials, and resource allocations differ between environments. Packaging production settings into the image would require a rebuild for another environment or expose those settings wherever the image was deployed. Baodium versioned the deployment configuration separately, and each release identified both the image digest and the configuration revision used with it. This idea is one of the Twelve-Factor App principles, a widely cited set of guidelines for building services that deploy cleanly across environments.

That separation would have exposed the missing environment variable from the original incident. The application also needed to reject invalid configuration before it accepted any work.

The approved range for the pool size is specific to this application, and it would come from a fleet-wide calculation like the one in Chapter 2. Validation should also cover formats, incompatible options, and required files. This check has a limit, though. A value being present says nothing about whether the endpoint is reachable or the credentials work, so those checks belong to initialization and dependency handling.

When validation fails, the error names the invalid field without printing its value, which matters for connection strings that contain credentials. The team also distinguished malformed configuration from a dependency that is temporarily unavailable. Retrying a network call cannot fix a missing required value, while a database that is briefly unreachable may justify a few bounded initialization retries or an instance that reports itself not ready, depending on the deployment policy.

Packaging the Deployment with Helm

The Kubernetes manifests for one service soon span several files, and most of their content is the same in every environment. Helm, a widely used package manager for Kubernetes, lets you write those manifests once as templates, called a chart, and supply the values that differ through a separate file for each environment. Baodium’s chart for Catalog Service placed the image reference, configuration, and resource settings in values files, so each environment’s differences were visible in one place and reviewed like any other code change.

The release pipeline fills in the image digest, so the chart always deploys the artifact that was tested. The pool size comes from the fleet-wide rule in Chapter 2. With twelve replicas and the rolling update later in this chapter allowing one extra Pod, at most thirteen instances can run concurrently, and an allocation of 300 database sessions divided by thirteen gives about 23 connections per instance.

Two details in this template solve production problems. First, the image line joins the repository and the digest, so a mutable tag cannot slip into a production deployment. Second, the config-revision annotation is a hash of the rendered ConfigMap. Kubernetes does not restart Pods when a ConfigMap they read changes, so without this annotation, a configuration change could go unused until the next unrelated deployment, or reach only the Pods that happened to restart. Because the hash is part of the Pod template, any configuration change produces a new template and a normal rolling update. The annotation also tells you which configuration revision each Pod is running, and the investigation commands at the end of this chapter rely on it.

Before applying a change, helm template renders the manifests locally so you can read what will be applied, and the helm-diff plugin shows what would change in the running cluster. Kustomize is a common alternative to Helm that patches plain manifests instead of templating them, and either works for the ideas in this chapter. Many teams also let a GitOps controller, such as Argo CD or Flux, apply the chart from Git, so that the cluster always matches the reviewed configuration and any manual change shows up as drift. Chapter 10 looks at how such changes are rolled out.

Secrets and Configuration Changes

Secrets are supplied through the deployment’s approved secret mechanism. They must not appear in image layers, build arguments, diagnostic dumps, or command-line arguments that may be recorded. Build arguments are a common mistake, because they are visible in the image’s build history. If a build step genuinely needs a credential, for example to download a private package, Docker BuildKit can mount it for that one step with RUN –mount=type=secret, and it never becomes part of a layer.

If a credential does end up in an image layer, deleting it in a later layer does not remove it, because image layers work like transparent sheets stacked on top of each other, and the earlier sheet still carries the file. Copies may also exist in registries, build caches, and on nodes, so the response has to include rotating the credential and tracking down those copies.

Rotation also needs a rule in the application. Updating a mounted file does not mean the process has reloaded it, and an environment variable does not change inside a running process just because the deployment definition changed. For each kind of configuration, the team decided whether a change required a restart or supported a validated reload, and the process reported the configuration revision it was using, without exposing any secret contents.

Container Isolation and Writable State

Container isolation limits which host resources a process can access and how much of them it can use. Linux namespaces give the process its own view of resources such as process IDs, mounts, and networking, and cgroups account for and limit its resource consumption. A container is these two kernel features applied to a process, and nothing more. There is no separate container object in the kernel.

How much isolation you get depends on the runtime configuration. Containers that share a network namespace, such as the containers in one Kubernetes Pod, also share its ports, and host mounts or elevated privileges can give a container far more access than the image alone suggests.

For Catalog Service, the runtime used a non-root user, dropped all Linux capabilities, and allowed writes only to named locations. Listing Listing shows those choices in a Kubernetes manifest.

The read-only root filesystem was especially useful during testing, because an accidental write to an application directory failed on the spot, during testing rather than in production. Directories that genuinely needed writes, such as /tmp, were mounted as separate volumes with a size limit.

The container’s writable layer disappears with the container. Replacing the container can discard anything written there, so Catalog Service stored business records in external storage and treated local files as temporary or rebuildable. That rule showed up in everyday features. A generated report needed durable object storage if customers were expected to download it later. A local cache could be discarded, but refilling it needed the admission controls from Chapter 5.

Temporary storage also needs a limit and monitoring. A service can fail because logs, downloads, or temporary files fill the available disk space, even when its CPU and memory measurements are normal. Kubernetes lets you set an ephemeral-storage request and limit for this, and it evicts a Pod that exceeds its limit.

CPU and Memory Configuration

On a shared host, someone has to decide how much CPU and memory each container may use. Containers turn that decision into configuration, and configuration becomes part of the conditions we have to test before release. Figure Figure shows what each kind of exhaustion looks like.

In Kubernetes, a resource request tells the scheduler how much capacity to reserve for a container, and a limit caps what the container may consume.

A CPU limit can cause throttling, while running out of memory can get the process killed. Base these values on measurements of the service under representative load. If you copy them from another application, you can create failures that resemble code regressions.

The example requests as much memory as the container is allowed to use. That makes its memory allocation predictable for placement and reduces the risk of eviction caused by using more than the request. CPU is different, because a service can be throttled when it uses more than its configured quota. Some teams omit CPU limits so containers can use available node CPU, but performance then depends on competing pods. The load test needs to reflect that choice.

CPU Throttling

Suppose Catalog Service passes a load test without a CPU limit, then runs in production with a restrictive quota. The kernel enforces a CPU limit as a quota of CPU time in each scheduling period, which is 100 milliseconds by default. A limit of one CPU allows 100 milliseconds of CPU time per period. If eight threads are busy concurrently, they use that quota in about 12.5 milliseconds, and the kernel then pauses the container for the other 87.5 milliseconds.

CPU throttling can lengthen requests without raising an application error, even when the node’s average CPU is low. The team compared throttled cgroup periods, the container quota, and CPU per request. If the application genuinely needed more CPU and the node had capacity, raising the limit was reasonable. An unexpected rise in CPU per request required an application investigation first.

Watch for runtimes that size themselves from the host. In Python, for example, os.cpu_count() returns the number of CPUs on the host, not the container’s CPU limit, so a server that starts one worker per CPU can start far more workers than its quota can run. Set the number of workers and threads from the container’s limits instead.

Memory Exhaustion

A container’s memory use includes much more than the application’s managed heap. Native allocations, thread stacks, buffers, runtime overhead, and memory-backed temporary storage all add to the memory that the limit applies to. If a language runtime is allowed to expand its heap to the entire container limit, these other allocations can get the process killed before the runtime reports its own heap as full. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM)’s MaxRAMPercentage setting, for example, exists so that you can leave room for this non-heap memory.

This mismatch is easy to create and hard to see in testing, because a test machine rarely enforces the same limit that production does. The engineers measured memory under realistic concurrency, large responses, and sustained operation, left room for non-heap use, and checked whether memory was released after work completed.

An out-of-memory termination needs evidence from the platform and the node. Exit status 137 only tells you that the process was killed with SIGKILL, since 137 is 128 plus the signal number 9. The exit code shows that a signal arrived, but not why it was sent. The termination reason, memory use, configured limits, node events, and restart timing help you tell a container that hit its own limit from a node-wide memory problem or an external kill.

Raising the limit may accommodate legitimate demand. If the application accumulates memory without a bound, however, a higher limit only postpones the next failure.

Finding Containers That Hit Their Limits

Limits that were right at release can become wrong as traffic and code change, so you need a routine way to find the containers that are running into them. Kubernetes records why each container last terminated, and the script in Listing Listing lists every container in the cluster whose last termination was an OOM kill, together with its memory limit, its restart total, and when it was killed.

Run it after an incident, or on a schedule, and you get a short list to investigate instead of scrolling through events. A none in the limit column is a finding in itself, because a container without a memory limit can use memory the scheduler never reserved for it.

For trends, metrics work better than snapshots. The queries in Listing Listing find containers whose memory working set is above 90 percent of their limit, and containers that are throttled in more than a quarter of their CPU periods. The working set is the memory measure the kubelet uses for eviction decisions. It excludes page cache that the kernel can reclaim, which makes it a closer match to what the OOM killer acts on than total memory usage.

Once you have found a container, resist raising its limit straight away. First look at its memory over the life of the process. Memory that rises steadily until the kill suggests a leak, while memory that rises with load and falls again suggests a limit that is too low for the work. If the limit really is too low, change it in the chart’s values file and let the normal deployment apply it. You could patch the live Deployment with kubectl set resources deployment/catalog -c catalog –limits=memory=1Gi, and during an incident that is sometimes the right emergency fix. It changes the cluster without changing Git, though, so the next deployment reverts it. If you patch the cluster during an incident, make the same change in the values file afterward.

For a recommendation based on observed usage, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA), an add-on maintained by the Kubernetes project, can run in a recommendation-only mode.

With updateMode set to "Off", the VPA never changes running Pods. It only publishes recommended requests, which you can read with kubectl describe vpa catalog and copy into the values file after review. Two cautions apply. A recommendation reflects past usage, so a memory leak inflates it, and the VPA should not manage the same resource that a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales on, because the two will work against each other.

Pod Placement and Scheduling Constraints

The scheduler decides which node each Pod runs on, and by default it looks mainly at resource requests. Several decisions from earlier chapters, however, depend on placement. A service has to survive the loss of an availability zone, as Chapter 2 described, each image has to run on the right CPU architecture, and demanding workloads need separate nodes. Kubernetes expresses these decisions through a few scheduling settings. You do not need to know all of them, but the ones in Listing Listing come up in almost every production service.

The topology spread constraint divides Catalog Service’s Pods evenly across availability zones, with no more than one Pod of difference between any two zones. Without it, the scheduler can put most replicas in one zone, and losing that zone removes far more than the third of capacity your N+1 calculation assumed. DoNotSchedule makes the rule strict, while ScheduleAnyway turns it into a preference the scheduler tries to honor.

The node selector restricts the Pods to x86 nodes. If you publish a multi-platform image, as described earlier, you can leave it out. A single-architecture image scheduled onto an ARM node, however, fails at startup with an “exec format error,” which resembles an application bug until someone checks the node.

The toleration and the node affinity work together to give Catalog Service its own pool of nodes. A taint on a node repels every Pod that does not tolerate it, and a label identifies the pool.

A toleration only allows a Pod onto tainted nodes. A toleration only permits the Pod to run on those nodes, and the node affinity sends it there. It requires the Pod to run on nodes labeled pool=catalog. Think of the taint as a “staff only” sign on a door, and the toleration as a staff badge. The badge lets you through the door, but it does not make you walk to it. The affinity is the instruction to go there. With both in place, Catalog Service runs only on its own nodes, and other workloads are excluded from them. Teams use the same pattern for nodes with graphics processing units (GPUs), local solid-state drives (SSDs), or unusually large amounts of memory.

Planned maintenance needs one more setting. When an operator cordons and evicts pods from a node to upgrade it, Kubernetes evicts the Pods on that node, and simultaneous maintenance on several nodes could evict many replicas. A PodDisruptionBudget limits that, much like a rule that only two cashiers may take a break at the same time.

With twelve replicas and minAvailable set to 10, planned evictions proceed only while at least ten Pods are available, so no more than two are removed at a time. A PodDisruptionBudget applies only to voluntary disruptions such as planned evictions. It does nothing during a crash or a node failure, so it complements failure-capacity planning rather than replacing it.

Decision review

Should readiness check the database?

Catalog Service cannot serve most of its endpoints without PostgreSQL. A reviewer proposes that the readiness probe run SELECT 1 against the database, so that an instance that has lost its connection stops receiving traffic. The service runs twelve replicas behind one load balancer.

Yes. An instance that cannot reach the database should not be sent requests.

No. Make readiness local, and let requests fail with a clear error when the database is unavailable.

Yes for a new instance during startup, but not afterward.

A helps when one instance has lost database access and other instances can still serve the request. During a shared database outage, however, all twelve probes could fail at once and remove every endpoint, including endpoints that could have served reduced responses or requests that do not need the database. The repeated probe queries also add work to the dependency.

B preserves those response paths during a shared outage. It still needs a way to detect a fault in one instance, such as a broken client pool, and a decision about whether removing that instance would improve service. An alert can report the fault, and the serving layer removes an instance only when its routing policy says to.

C checks connectivity at startup but cannot detect a later failure in one instance. The startup probe in this chapter checks local initialization, so adding a database check would be a separate policy choice, with its own limits on query frequency and startup waiting.

Choose readiness behavior by testing both failures, one isolated instance and the shared database. Route requests to instances that can serve the required response, including an approved fallback. No single dependency probe can establish that for every endpoint.

Startup, Readiness, and Liveness Probes

A process can be running without being ready for the traffic it is about to receive, in the same way that a restaurant can have its lights on before the kitchen is ready to cook. Catalog Service needed valid configuration, completed local initialization, and working database access before it could serve its first requests, but it did not need every optional cache entry to be filled.

Kubernetes gives you three probes, and each one checks something different (Table Table). The startup probe gives initialization time to finish. The readiness probe decides whether this instance should receive new traffic. The liveness probe looks for a condition that restarting the container would fix.

Probe results have different operational consequences.
Check What it establishes Consequence of failure
Startup Initialization has completed within its allowed startup period. Continued failure can trigger a restart.
Readiness This instance should receive service traffic. The serving layer removes it from eligible endpoints.
Liveness The process is not in a condition that warrants a restart. Continued failure can trigger a restart.

Kubernetes does not run the liveness and readiness probes until the startup probe succeeds, so the startup allowance should cover the startup times you have measured, including slow ones. A process that has not loaded its required configuration should never become ready. An empty optional cache, on the other hand, need not block readiness if bounded source reads can handle the initial load.

Liveness needs particular care. You know the classic IT advice, “have you tried turning it off and on again?” It works only for problems that a restart fixes, and a liveness probe should check only those problems. If the liveness probe checks a shared dependency, a database outage makes every instance fail the probe, and Kubernetes restarts all of them. Restarting Catalog Service does not repair PostgreSQL, and simultaneous restarts add connection setup and cache loading to the outage. Limit liveness to the process itself, such as a deadlocked event loop, handle dependency failures in the request path, and make every probe inexpensive so that the probes do not become a source of load themselves.

Warm-Up and Initial Traffic Admission

An instance can be ready before it has reached full operating capacity. A new process may have few open database connections, an empty local cache, or a runtime that has not yet compiled its frequently used code paths, so its first requests can cost more than requests to an established instance. Once readiness succeeds, the serving layer may send the instance its full share of traffic without any ramp. Some load balancers offer a slow-start mode that increases a new instance’s share gradually, for example the slow-start setting on AWS Application Load Balancer target groups or Envoy’s slow-start configuration, which lets some warm-up continue while traffic rises.

A rule such as “ready once 20 database connections are open” is a weak readiness check. The connections have to be usable, and the number should come from the expected initial demand and the cost of opening connections. Opening the entire pool before serving can waste sessions and create a burst of connection setup across the fleet during a rollout.

Warm-up work also needs limits, because new, existing, and terminating instances all use the same database during a deployment. As Chapter 5 pointed out, a shared Redis cache does not empty when one application process restarts, but local in-process caches do, so any warming plan has to identify which cache needs filling.

For a Kubernetes rollout, a strategy like this one controls planned replacement.

This asks for no planned reduction in available replicas and allows one extra Pod during replacement, which is much tighter than the default of 25 percent you saw in Chapter 2. An old process may still be shutting down while its replacement starts, so for a short time more than one extra process can be using resources. Terminating Pods may still use resources, and autoscaling, node replacement, or another deployment can add more work, so the database allocation must allow for those overlaps.

If no node has room for the extra Pod, the rollout may stall. That is better than assuming that a desired number of replicas proves the capacity for replacement exists. Chapter 10 treats a deployment as a controlled experiment, with canaries and automated comparison between versions. Here, the concern is only the resources that replacement uses.

Graceful Shutdown and In-Flight Requests

Replacing an instance requires coordination with the process already serving requests. The old instance needs time to finish eligible work and release resources before Kubernetes terminates it. A shop closing for the night provides a useful comparison. Staff lock the door to new customers, serve the people already inside, and only then turn off the lights. When Catalog Service received a termination signal, it did the same. It marked itself unavailable for new traffic, let accepted requests finish, closed its clients, and exited within a bounded shutdown deadline. This is usually called a graceful shutdown.

Locking the door takes a moment to reach every entrance, though. Proxies and clients receive the news of an endpoint’s removal at different times, and existing connections may deliver requests for a while longer. In Kubernetes, the Pod receives SIGTERM at about the same time as its endpoint removal starts propagating, so a process that exits as soon as the signal arrives can drop requests that were still on their way. A common remedy is a short pause before shutdown begins, as in the preStop hook below.

The grace period includes the time spent in the preStop hook, so the pause and the draining both have to fit within 30 seconds in this example. The exec form also needs a sleep binary in the image, and recent Kubernetes versions offer a built-in sleep action for minimal images that do not include one.

The process also has to receive and handle the termination signal, which brings back the PID 1 issue from earlier in the chapter. This is another reason to test the actual entrypoint and any wrapper scripts in the image.

If a request cannot finish before the process is forcibly terminated, the outcome depends on the operation. A read can fail and be retried under the caller’s policy, while a payment write may need the durable reconciliation procedure from Chapter 3.

A longer grace period allows more draining, but it also extends the time during which old and new instances use resources together, so shutdown duration belongs in the deployment capacity calculation. The replacement test sent representative requests while terminating an instance and checked errors, unfinished operations, resource release, and how long the process took to exit.

Image Rollback and External State

An earlier image digest is only a usable rollback target when the old application can still read the database and configuration left by the new version. Removing a database column may break the previous image even when the container starts successfully. The same concern applies to event formats and secrets that were rotated for security reasons.

We therefore test representative requests from the previous artifact against the expected post-release data and configuration. The expand-then-contract migration and rollback gates are developed in Chapter 10. Undoing an image also does not undo a completed payment or another external business effect. Those outcomes require a separate reconciliation or compensation procedure.

Deployment Identity and Failure Diagnosis

In the original incident, the engineers had to inspect hosts by hand, because the release record identified only the application revision. The revised record included the image digest, source revision, configuration revision, resource settings, and platform-specific artifact, and startup events recorded where each instance ran and how its initialization went. The config-revision annotation from the Helm chart made the configuration comparable across instances.

With that information, an engineer can make a focused comparison during an incident. The commands in Listing Listing are all read-only, which matters when the instinct under pressure is to restart something before anyone understands what differs.

The investigation begins with the deployed image and configuration, then checks Kubernetes events and the process failure. This distinguishes a packaging or placement error from an application regression. If step 1 shows two digests, the question is about the state of the rollout, and the later steps can wait. If the image digests and configuration revisions all match, the engineers look at differences in host configuration and runtime conditions, and step 4 shows whether the failures occur on one node or several.

If failures cluster on one node even though the artifact and configuration match, the next things to examine are that node’s resources, its kernel and runtime, its mounts, and its networking. A shared image can still interact badly with one host’s conditions, so matching digests narrow the investigation without proving that the application is not involved.

Secret values do not belong in diagnostic output. Compare configuration using names, presence, approved non-secret fields, and versioned references. Dumping the entire environment into logs can turn a deployment investigation into a credential exposure.

Summary

The phrase “it works on my machine” usually means that the source code was the only thing two environments shared. The lasting fix is to make the thing you deploy carry its own runtime, and to name it unambiguously, so that two people can be sure they are talking about the same artifact. A container image promoted by digest does that.

The image is only part of a running service, though, and most of this chapter is about the other part. Configuration and secrets arrive from outside. CPU and memory limits decide whether a busy moment becomes throttling or a restart. Placement decides whether losing a node or a zone takes the service with it. Probes decide when Kubernetes sends traffic and when it restarts a process, and shutdown decides whether accepted work finishes. When some replicas work and others fail, compare the image digest, the configuration revision, and the node first. Those three facts separate an artifact problem from an environment problem faster than any log search.

Containers made Catalog reproducible. The database behind it was about to become the constraint, and Chapter 7 takes Baodium into the point where reads outgrow a single primary.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The tested image, combined with validated configuration and declared runtime conditions, can support the traffic assigned to each instance.
Condition that tests it & A deployment changes configuration, resource limits, or probe outcomes.
Constraint or invariant & The image contains the application’s user space. The deployment and host supply configuration, mounts, kernel behavior, resource enforcement, networking, and external services.
Evidence and uncertainty & The original failures were confined to hosts with different system libraries, language runtimes, or required configuration, despite a shared application revision.

Still unknown: whether initialization, resource limits, host differences, and current external state allow the approved artifact and its rollback version to serve representative requests.
Signal and evaluation window & Compare image digests and configuration revisions at release. Measure throttling, OOM events, and readiness throughout the rollout.
Control and decision & Promote the tested artifact by digest with versioned configuration. Admit traffic only after the required initialization checks, and verify replacement and rollback against current external state.
Owner and review trigger & The service owner defines initialization, readiness, shutdown, and compatibility requirements. The platform owner manages artifact delivery, runtime policy, placement, and resource enforcement. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.

  1. An image tag such as latest can be reassigned to a different image. A digest identifies the image content the registry returns, which makes artifact promotion and rollback reproducible.↩︎
